cards.title: OIL RIG
body: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain — of electrons. Oxidising agent is the thief (it is itself reduced).

cards.title: The Nature of Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
body: Oxidation number rises when a species is oxidised. Example: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ (ox). Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (red).

cards.title: 2.1.1 The Different Definitions of Oxidation and Reduction
body: **The oxidation number** is the electrical charge assigned to each atom in a given compound.
Even when atoms of an element are bonded together to form molecules, they have a zero oxidation number.
Examples: Na, Ca, N2, O2, etc. have zero oxidation numbers.
Rule 5: The sum of the oxidation numbers of the atoms in a compound is zero.

cards.title: 2.1.2 Determining Oxidation Numbers of Common Elements
body: Rule 2: The oxidation number of any simple metal ion or nonmetal ion is equal to the charge on the ion.
The oxidation number of hydrogen is +1 (citing rule 4).
The oxidation number of oxygen is –2 (citing rule 3).
Rule 6: In a poly atomic ion (radical), the sum of the oxidation numbers of the atoms equals the charge on the ion.

cards.title: 2.1.3 Oxidizing and Reducing Agents
body: In general, chemical reactions can be grouped into two types based on the change of the oxidation numbers (the transfer of electrons).
Oxidation-reduction reactions (redox reactions), and non-oxidation reduction reactions (non-redox reactions).
Redox reactions involve a transfer of electrons (a change in oxidation numbers).
Non-redox reactions do not show a change in oxidation numbers.

cards.title: 2.1.4 Writing and Balancing Simple Redox Equations
body: Two methods are used to balance redox chemical equations.
The other is based on splitting the redox reaction into two half-reactions – one involving oxidation and the other involving reduction.
In writing equations for redox reactions, just as for other reactions, the compositions and formulas of the substances that react, and of the products that are formed, must be known.
Step 1: Identify the oxidation number of each atom involved in the reaction.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Identify the reducing agent in the following displacement reaction: $$Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Assign oxidation numbers**
Reactants: $$Fe = 0$$, $$Cu = +2$$, $$S = +6$$, $$O = -2$$
Products: $$Fe = +2$$, $$S = +6$$, $$O = -2$$, $$Cu = 0$$

**Step 2: Identify species undergoing changes**
$$Fe$$ goes from $$0$$ to $$+2$$ (oxidized).
$$Cu^{2+}$$ goes from $$+2$$ to $$0$$ (reduced).

**Step 3: Identify the reducing agent**
The species that is oxidized acts as the reducing agent because it donates electrons. Since $$Fe(s)$$ is oxidized, it is the reducing agent.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The reducing agent is **$$Fe(s)$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: During the electrolysis of molten lead bromide ($$PbBr_2$$), what product is formed at the negative cathode?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify ions present in molten lead bromide**
The molten state contains only $$Pb^{2+}$$ and $$Br^-$$ ions.

**Step 2: Determine which ion migrates to the negative cathode**
Cations (positively charged) migrate to the negative cathode. Thus, $$Pb^{2+}$$ migrates to the cathode.

**Step 3: Determine the reaction at the cathode**
At the cathode, reduction occurs: $$Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb(s)$$.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The product at the cathode is **Lead metal ($$Pb$$)**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the oxidation number of sulfur ($$S$$) in sulfuric acid ($$H_2SO_4$$)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Assign known oxidation numbers**
Hydrogen is assigned $$+1$$ and oxygen is assigned $$-2$$.

**Step 2: Setup the algebraic sum for a neutral compound**
The sum of the oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule must equal zero.
$$2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0$$

**Step 3: Solve for $$x$$**
$$2 + x - 8 = 0 \implies x - 6 = 0 \implies x = +6$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The oxidation number of sulfur in $$H_2SO_4$$ is **$$+6$$**.

Mnemonic — “An Ox, Red Cat”
body: Anode = oxidation. Reduction = cathode. In a galvanic cell the anode is negative; in electrolysis the anode is the positive electrode (attached to + of the pack).

cards.title: Electrolysis
body: Electrochemical series: metals high up donate e⁻ easily (reactive, good reducing agents). A metal will displace a metal *below* it from solution.

cards.title: 2.2.1 What is Electrolysis?
body: **Electrolysis** is the process in which electrical energy is used to cause a non-spontaneous chemical reaction to occur.
**An electrolytic cell** is an apparatus for carrying out electrolysis.
The electrolytic cell consists of an electrolyte, electrodes and a source of electricity.
The electric source for electrolysis should be a direct current (DC) or small batteries (e.g., a few 1.5V cells in series).

cards.title: 2.2.2 The Mechanism of Electrolysis
body: The conduction of electricity through an electrolyte (either molten or aqueous state) is due to the migration of the ions towards their oppositely charged electrodes.
During the electrolysis, a battery or other DC sources move electrons through the wire to the electrodes.
The electrons enter the electrolyte through the cathode; positively charged ions (cations) move to the negative electrode (cathode) and thus receive electrons and are reduced.
After electrolysis, at both electrodes, the ions are converted into neutral atoms Therefore, there is a transfer of electrons between the electrodes and the ions.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Electrolysis of Molten Electrolytes
body: Lead bromide can be used to demonstrate the electrolysis of molten electrolytes because it has fairly lower melting point.
Decomposition of the electrolyte into its ions by heat.
Discharge of the ions into their respective neutral substances at the surface of the electrodes, that is, reduction takes place at the cathode.
The atoms of lead are deposited at the surface of cathode with characteristic grayish color.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions of Electrolytes
body: In the electrolysis of aqueous solutions, not only the electrolyte but also water dissociates (slightly), so the ions from water (H⁺ and OH⁻) compete with the ions of the electrolyte at the electrodes.
For example, an aqueous solution of NaCl contains four ions: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from sodium chloride, and H⁺ and OH⁻ from water.
Which ion is discharged depends on three factors: (1) its position in the electrochemical series, (2) its relative concentration, (3) the nature of the electrode.
Keeping the other factors constant, the cation that most readily accepts electrons is discharged: with Na⁺ and H⁺ present, H⁺ is discharged; with Cu²⁺ and H⁺ present, Cu²⁺ is discharged.

cards.title: 2.2.4 (2) Relative concentration of the ions, step by step
body: In a solution there are always **two possible cations** (the metal ion and H⁺ from water) and **two possible anions** (the acid ion and OH⁻ from water). Only one of each is discharged. The first rule (position in the electrochemical series) is not the only rule: **concentration** can change the winner.
**Step 1 — List all the ions,** from the salt and from water. For NaCl(aq): Na⁺, Cl⁻ from the salt; H⁺, OH⁻ from water.
**Step 2 — Cathode (−):** compare the cations. Na⁺ is very high in the series and very hard to discharge, so **H⁺ is discharged** even when Na⁺ is far more concentrated — here the position wins.
$$2\mathrm{H^{+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$$

**Step 3 — Anode (+):** compare the anions. OH⁻ is easier to discharge than Cl⁻. **But** if Cl⁻ is present at a **much higher concentration** (brine, concentrated HCl) Cl⁻ is discharged instead — here the concentration wins.
$$2\mathrm{Cl^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}$$
**Step 4 — Decide what is left in solution.** In brine the H⁺ and Cl⁻ leave; Na⁺ and OH⁻ stay → the solution becomes **sodium hydroxide**.
$$2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}$$

**Dilute NaCl(aq) is different:** with little Cl⁻, OH⁻ is discharged and **oxygen** is formed: \(4\mathrm{OH^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} + 4\mathrm{e^{-}}\). Overall only water is decomposed: \(2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\), and the salt solution slowly gets more concentrated.
**Concentrated hydrochloric acid** behaves like brine at the anode: H₂ at the cathode, Cl₂ at the anode: \(2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)}\).

cards.title: Model: dilute vs concentrated sodium chloride

states.label: Dilute NaCl
states.text: Cathode: H₂. Anode: OH⁻ is discharged → O₂. Water is used up; NaCl is left more concentrated.

states.label: Brine
states.text: Cathode: H₂. Anode: the huge excess of Cl⁻ wins → Cl₂. Na⁺ and OH⁻ stay behind → NaOH(aq).

cards.title: 2.2.4 (3) Nature of the electrode, step by step
body: The electrode material is the **least important** factor, but in two cases it decides the product.
**Case 1 — Mercury cathode with brine.** On mercury, H⁺ is very slow to discharge, while sodium dissolves in the mercury as an **amalgam**. So **Na⁺** is discharged instead of H⁺:
$$\mathrm{Na^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na(s)}$$
$$\mathrm{Na(s)} + \mathrm{Hg(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaHg(l)}$$

The anode (graphite) still gives Cl₂. The amalgam is later treated with water to give very pure NaOH and H₂: \(2\mathrm{NaHg(l)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{Hg(l)}\).
**Case 2 — Copper(II) sulphate with an inert vs a copper anode.** The cathode is the same in both cells (Cu²⁺ is lower than H⁺ in the series, so copper is deposited):
$$\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}$$

**Graphite or platinum anode (inert):** SO₄²⁻ is not discharged, OH⁻ is → oxygen: \(4\mathrm{OH^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} + 4\mathrm{e^{-}}\). The blue colour fades and the solution becomes acidic (H₂SO₄ is left).

**Copper anode (active):** neither anion is discharged. The copper atoms of the anode lose electrons more easily, so **the anode dissolves**: \(\mathrm{Cu(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}\). No gas forms; the blue colour stays the same, because every Cu²⁺ removed at the cathode is replaced at the anode.
**Correction:** the textbook says the mercury-cathode example uses “molten sodium chloride”. It is **aqueous** sodium chloride (brine) — in a melt there is no H⁺ to compete with.

cards.title: Model: CuSO₄(aq) with an inert and with a copper anode

states.label: Graphite anode
states.text: Anode: oxygen bubbles. Cu²⁺ is used up, so the blue fades and H₂SO₄ is left.

states.label: Copper anode
states.text: Anode: copper dissolves, no gas. Cu²⁺ in = Cu²⁺ out, so the blue stays.

head: Factor
Rule
Example

H⁺ before Na⁺; Cu²⁺ before H⁺; OH⁻ before SO₄²⁻
a much more concentrated ion can be discharged instead

cards.title: Worked example: predicting products step by step
cards.problem: Predict the products at each inert electrode for (a) concentrated KCl(aq), (b) dilute H₂SO₄, (c) AgNO₃(aq). Write the half-equations.

steps.text: (a) Ions K⁺, H⁺, Cl⁻, OH⁻. Cathode: K⁺ is very high in the series → H⁺: \(2\mathrm{H^{+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}\). Anode: concentrated Cl⁻ → \(2\mathrm{Cl^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}\); KOH is left.
(b) Ions H⁺, SO₄²⁻, OH⁻. Cathode: H₂. Anode: OH⁻ before SO₄²⁻ → \(4\mathrm{OH^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} + 4\mathrm{e^{-}}\). Volume ratio H₂ : O₂ = 2 : 1.
(c) Ions Ag⁺, H⁺, NO₃⁻, OH⁻. Cathode: Ag⁺ is below H⁺ → \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag(s)}\). Anode: OH⁻ before NO₃⁻ → O₂; HNO₃ is left.

cards.answer: (a) H₂ / Cl₂; (b) H₂ / O₂; (c) Ag / O₂

cards.title: 2.2.5 Applications of Electrolysis
body: Electrolysis has four main applications: (1) electroplating, (2) preparation of gases (H₂, O₂, Cl₂) and extraction of reactive metals (Na, Mg, Al), (3) purification (refining) of metals such as copper, (4) manufacture of sodium hydroxide from brine.

Activity 2.7: dissolve about three teaspoons of copper(II) chloride in 150 mL of water in a 250 mL beaker, dip in two carbon rods and connect a 6 V battery. Do not touch bare wires or short-circuit the battery.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Applications of electrolysis, step by step
body: Electrolysis is used to coat objects, to make gases and alkalis, to extract reactive metals and to purify metals. In every application ask the same questions: **what is the cathode, the anode and the electrolyte?** and **which ions are discharged?**
**1 · Electroplating** — coating an object with a thin layer of another metal, to prevent rusting or to make it look better (silver or gold on spoons and jewellery, chromium on taps, tin on cans).
• **Cathode (−):** the object to be plated. • **Anode (+):** the plating metal. • **Electrolyte:** a solution of a salt of the plating metal.

For silver plating (AgNO₃ electrolyte): cathode \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag(s)}\), anode \(\mathrm{Ag(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{e^{-}}\). The anode dissolves as fast as silver is deposited, so the electrolyte stays the same.

**2 · Preparation of gases and extraction of metals** — Cl₂ and H₂ from brine; O₂ and H₂ from acidified water. Very reactive metals (Na, K, Ca, Mg, Al) cannot be reduced by carbon, so they are extracted by electrolysis of their **molten** compounds.
Sodium from molten NaCl: cathode \(\mathrm{Na^{+}(l)} + \mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na(l)}\), anode \(2\mathrm{Cl^{-}(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}\).

Aluminium: Al₂O₃ is dissolved in molten **cryolite** (Na₃AlF₆) to lower the working temperature (from about 2050 °C to about 950 °C). Cathode \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}(l)} + 3\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al(l)}\), anode \(2\mathrm{O^{2-}(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} + 4\mathrm{e^{-}}\). The hot carbon anodes burn away, \(\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\), and must be replaced.

**3 · Purification (refining) of copper** — impure copper is the **anode**, a thin sheet of pure copper is the **cathode**, the electrolyte is CuSO₄(aq) with a little H₂SO₄. Copper dissolves from the anode and is deposited on the cathode (99.99 % pure). Less reactive impurities (Ag, Au, Pt) fall as **anode mud**; more reactive ones (Zn, Fe) stay in solution.

**4 · Manufacture of sodium hydroxide** — electrolysis of brine gives three useful products at once: \(2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{H_{2}(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}\). NaOH is used for soap, paper and textiles; Cl₂ for water treatment and PVC; H₂ for margarine and ammonia.

cards.title: Model: electroplating a spoon with silver (Fig. 2.6)

steps.text: **Anode (+): pure silver** — silver atoms lose electrons and go into solution.
**Cathode (−): the spoon** — Ag⁺ ions gain electrons; a thin, even silver layer forms.
**Electrolyte:** Ag⁺ ions carry the current through the solution; their concentration stays constant.
**Anode (+): impure copper** gets thinner: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.
**Anode mud:** silver, gold and platinum do not dissolve and collect under the anode — they are valuable by-products.

cards.title: Electroplating and refining compared
head: Electroplating (silver)
Refining copper
body: In both, the anode is a metal that dissolves (an active anode). The difference is the purpose and what the cathode is.

cards.title: Worked example: design a nickel-plating cell
cards.problem: You want to nickel-plate an iron key. Name the anode, cathode and electrolyte and write the electrode equations.

steps.text: The object to be coated is always the **cathode** → the iron key (cleaned).
The plating metal is the **anode** → a nickel bar.
The electrolyte must contain the plating ions → nickel(II) sulphate solution.

cards.answer: Anode Ni, cathode key, electrolyte NiSO₄(aq)

cards.title: Worked example: why aluminium needs electrolysis and cryolite
cards.problem: Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis, why cryolite is used, and why the anodes must be replaced.

steps.text: Al is above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce Al₂O₃.
Pure Al₂O₃ melts at about 2050 °C — too costly; dissolved in molten cryolite it conducts at about 950 °C.
Oxygen formed at the hot carbon anodes reacts with them: \(\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\), so they burn away.

cards.answer: Too reactive for carbon; cryolite lowers the temperature; anodes burn.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In electroplating, the object to be plated is made the …
cards.why: Metal ions are positive and are reduced at the negative electrode, the cathode — so the object must be the cathode.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In copper refining the anode mud contains …
cards.why: Metals less reactive than copper (Ag, Au, Pt) do not dissolve at the anode and fall to the bottom.

cards.title: 2.2.6 Faraday’s Law of Electrolysis
body: The quantitative relationship between the amount of electricity passed through an electrolytes solution and the extent of the product is given by Faraday’s laws.
Faraday’s First Law of Electrolysis states that the mass of a substance produced by electrolysis is proportional to the quantity of electricity used.

Faraday's second law states that the mass of two substances that are deposited or liberated from electrodes, given the same applied electrical charge, is directly proportional to the equivalent masses of the two substances.

cards.title: 2.2.6 Faraday's laws, step by step
body: Faraday's laws connect the **amount of electricity** passed with the **amount of product** at an electrode. Every calculation starts from the **half-equation**, because it tells you how many electrons each ion needs.
**Step 1 — Charge passed:** $$Q = I \times t$$ with I in amperes and t in **seconds** (1 C = 1 A s).
**Step 2 — Moles of electrons:** one mole of electrons carries **1 faraday, F = 96 500 C**. $$n(e^-) = \frac{Q}{F}$$
**Step 3 — Use the half-equation:** z = the charge on the ion = electrons per atom.
$$\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag(s)} \qquad \text{1 mol e}^- \to \text{1 mol Ag}$$
$$\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)} \qquad \text{2 mol e}^- \to \text{1 mol Cu}$$
$$\mathrm{Al^{3+}(l)} + 3\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al(l)} \qquad \text{3 mol e}^- \to \text{1 mol Al}$$
**Step 4 — Mass:** moles of metal × molar mass. All steps together give the textbook formula:
$$m = \frac{A}{z}\cdot\frac{I\,t}{F} = \frac{\text{Eq. mass} \times I \times t}{96\,500}$$
**First law:** m ∝ Q (double the current or the time → double the mass). The constant k = A/(zF) is the **electrochemical equivalent** (mass deposited by 1 C).
**Second law:** for the **same charge** (cells in series), the masses are in the ratio of the **equivalent masses** A/z: $$\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{A_1/z_1}{A_2/z_2}$$

**Gases:** same method; at room conditions 1 mol of gas occupies about 24 dm³. \(2\mathrm{Cl^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cl_{2}(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}}\) → 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cl₂; \(4\mathrm{OH^{-}(aq)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{O_{2}(g)} + 4\mathrm{e^{-}}\) → 4 mol e⁻ per mol O₂.

cards.title: Model: two cells in series (second law)

steps.text: **Silver cell:** \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq)} + \mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag(s)}\) — every mole of electrons deposits 108 g of silver.
**Nickel cell:** \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ni(s)}\) — every mole of electrons deposits only ½ mol = 29.5 g of nickel.
**Same wire, same current, same time → same Q.** So mass(Ag) : mass(Ni) = 108 : 29.5.

cards.title: Worked example 3: silver and nickel in series (second law)
cards.problem: Two cells, AgNO₃(aq) and Ni(NO₃)₂(aq), are in series. 2.16 g of silver is deposited in the first cell. What mass of nickel is deposited in the second? (Ag = 108, Ni = 59)

steps.text: Note: the textbook also says 1.5 A for 10 min (900 C). That charge would deposit only 1.01 g Ag and 0.275 g Ni, so its data do not agree; 2.16 g needs 1930 C (1.5 A for about 21.4 min). In the textbook, “Z_Ag = 108, Z_Ni = 59” are the **atomic masses**, not charges.

steps.text: Correction: the textbook gives Cr = 62 and 8.4 A. The molar mass of chromium is **52 g/mol**; with 52 and 8.4 A the ratio is 2.5 (not a whole number), so the current must be 10.0 A, as in the original version of this problem.

cards.title: Tips and common mistakes
body: Always convert time to seconds (min × 60, h × 3600).
Write the half-equation first — z is the number of electrons in it, not the group number.
The second law only works when the cells are in series (same charge).

cards.title: Worked: agent roles
cards.problem: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, what is reduced?

cards.title: Quick check

options.A: Reduction takes place at the cathode
options.C: Both oxidation and reduction takes place at the anode
options.E: Oxidation takes place at the cathode

cards.why:
In any electrochemical cell, including electrolysis:
1. **Reduction** always occurs at the **cathode** (gain of electrons).
2. **Oxidation** always occurs at the **anode** (loss of electrons).
3. Cations (positive) move toward the cathode (negative electrode).
4. Anions (negative) move toward the anode (positive electrode).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following species is produced at the cathode when an aqueous solution of potassium chloride is electrolyzed using carbon electrodes?
cards.why: In aqueous $$KCl$$, both $$K^+$$ and $$H^+$$ (from water) move to the cathode. Since $$H^+$$ is lower in the electrochemical series, it is more easily reduced than $$K^+$$. Therefore, **hydrogen gas ($$H_2$$)** is produced instead of potassium metal.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the molten electrolysis of $$ NaBr $$ the product liberated at the anode is:
cards.why:
In molten electrolysis, there are only two ions: $$ Na^+ $$ and $$ Br^- $$.

- **At the Cathode (Reduction):** Positive ions ($$ Na^+ $$) move here to gain electrons: $$ Na^+ + e^- \rightarrow Na(l) $$.
- **At the Anode (Oxidation):** Negative ions ($$ Br^- $$) move here to lose electrons: $$ 2Br^- \rightarrow Br_2(g) + 2e^- $$.

Therefore, Bromine gas ($$ Br_2 $$) is liberated at the anode.

glossary.meaning: Loss of electrons (an increase in oxidation number), or gain of oxygen.
The oxidation number is the electrical charge assigned to each atom in a given compound.
Electrolysis is the process in which electrical energy is used to cause a non-spontaneous chemical reaction to occur.
An electrolyte is a compound that conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water.
Describes a substance that has lost electrons; it acts as the reducing agent.
An electrolytic cell is an apparatus for carrying out electrolysis.
Using electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of metal; the object is the cathode.
Water is a weak electrolyte and is only slightly dissociated.
An alloy of a metal with mercury, e.g. sodium amalgam NaHg formed at a mercury cathode.
The insoluble impurities (Ag, Au, Pt) that collect below the anode in copper refining.
Atomic mass ÷ charge on the ion (A/z); the mass deposited by one mole of electrons.
The charge on one mole of electrons, F = 96 500 C/mol.

tips.text: The traditional method is limited to reactions that involve oxygen and hydrogen only.
The atom that gains an electron or electrons is said to be reduced, whereas the atom that loses an electron or electrons(s) is said to be oxidized.
An element that oxidizes another species, it itself being reduced, is called an oxidizing agent; an element that reduces another species, it being oxidized, is called a reducing agent.
An element that is oxidized is called a reducing agent, while an element that is reduced is called an oxidizing agent.

Oxidation – reduction reactions (also called redox reactions), involve the transfer of electrons from one species to another (a change in oxidation number). Some reactions do not show a change in oxidation numbers, these are called non-redox reactions.
There is one branch of chemistry called electrochemistry that studies the relationship between chemical energy and electrical energy.
The two main kinds of reaction in electrochemistry are electrochemical reactions and electrolysis.
In electrochemical reactions, chemical energy is converted into electrical energy. However, in electrolysis an electrical energy is used to bring about a chemical reaction.
Electrolysis is the process in which electrical energy is used to cause a non-spontaneous chemical reaction to occur.
An electrolytic cell is an apparatus for carrying out electrolysis.

questions.q: __________ is defined as a gaining of electron by a substance.
why:
In chemistry, the transfer of electrons is described by two processes:
- **Oxidation:** Loss of electrons.
- **Reduction:** Gain of electrons.

Memory Aid: **OIL RIG** (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).

**Result:** A
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The oxidizing and reducing agents in the reaction: $$ Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s) $$, are______and______respectively.
why:
**Step 1: Assign oxidation numbers.**
- $$ Fe $$: 0 to +2 (Oxidized)
- $$ Cu $$: +2 to 0 (Reduced)
**Step 2: Identify agents.**
- The substance that is oxidized is the **reducing agent** ($$ Fe $$).
- The substance that is reduced is the **oxidizing agent** ($$ CuSO_4 $$ or $$ Cu^{2+} $$).
Order requested: Oxidizing agent, then Reducing agent -> $$ CuSO_4 $$ and $$ Fe $$.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Reduction is a process of:
why:
In Redox chemistry, **Reduction** is defined as the **gain of electrons**. 
- Mnemonic: **OIL RIG** (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: A reduction reaction is:

options.A: Takes place at anode during electrolysis.

why:
**Step 1:** Define Reduction using the OIL RIG mnemonic (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons).
**Step 2:** Evaluate options:
- A: Oxidation occurs at the anode (AnOx).
- B: Oxidation involves an increase in oxidation number; Reduction involves a decrease.
- C: Reduction is the gain of electrons. (Correct)
- D: Addition of oxygen is Oxidation.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The oxidation number of N in $$ Mg(NO_3)_2 $$ is:
why:
1. $$ Mg(NO_3)_2 $$ dissociates into $$ Mg^{2+} $$ and two $$ NO_3^- $$ ions.
2. Let's find N in the nitrate ion ($$ NO_3^- $$).
3. Rule: Sum of oxidation numbers in an ion equals its charge.
$$ x (N) + 3(-2) (O) = -1 $$
$$ x - 6 = -1 $$
$$ x = +5 $$
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: In the reaction $$Zn(s) + 2AgNO_3(aq) \rightarrow Zn(NO_3)_2(aq) + 2Ag(s)$$, Zn is
why:
**Step 1:** Zinc ($$Zn$$) goes from an oxidation state of 0 to +2. LEO (Losing Electrons = Oxidation).
**Step 2:** A substance that is oxidized acts as the **reducing agent** because it provides electrons to reduce the other substance ($$Ag^+$$ to $$Ag$$).
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The oxidation number of chlorine in $$ClO_3^-$$ is
why:
**Step 1:** Set up the equation. The sum of oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion equals its charge ($$-1$$).
**Step 2:** Oxygen usually has an oxidation number of $$-2$$.
**Step 3:** $$Cl + 3(O) = -1$$
**Step 4:** $$Cl + 3(-2) = -1 \Rightarrow Cl - 6 = -1$$
**Step 5:** $$Cl = -1 + 6 = +5$$.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which of the following reactions represents an oxidation reaction?
why:
**Step 1:** Define oxidation. Oxidation is the loss of electrons or an increase in the oxidation state of an element.
**Step 2:** Analyze Option C. Sulphur ($$ S $$) has an oxidation state of 0 as an element. In $$ SO_2 $$, Oxygen is -2, so Sulphur must be +4. 
**Result:** Since the oxidation state of Sulphur increases from 0 to +4, it is being oxidized.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of **Br** in **KBrO**?
why:
**Step 1: Assign known oxidation numbers.**
- Potassium ($$ K $$) is always $$ +1 $$ (Group 1).
- Oxygen ($$ O $$) is usually $$ -2 $$.

**Step 2: Set up the equation for the neutral compound (sum = 0).**
- $$ (+1) + Br + (-2) = 0 $$
- $$ Br - 1 = 0 $$
- $$ Br = +1 $$

**Result:** B
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The oxidation number of chlorine in $$ ClO_4^- $$ is
why:
**Step 1: Set up the equation.**
The sum of oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion equals its charge (-1).
Let $$ Cl = x $$. Oxygen is usually -2.

**Step 2: Solve for x.**
$$ x + 4(-2) = -1 $$
$$ x - 8 = -1 $$
$$ x = -1 + 8 = +7 $$
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of dilute NaCl(aq) with inert electrodes, the products are …
why: Step 1: cathode — H⁺ is discharged before Na⁺ → H₂.
Step 2: anode — in dilute solution OH⁻ is discharged before Cl⁻ → O₂.
Step 3: so H₂ and O₂ (water is decomposed).
questions.tip: Dilute → O₂; concentrated chloride → Cl₂.
questions.label: 2.2.4 Electrolysis of aqueous solutions

questions.q: Explain why sodium (not hydrogen) is discharged at a mercury cathode in the electrolysis of brine. Write the equations.
questions.answer: On mercury H⁺ is discharged only very slowly, while sodium dissolves in mercury to form an amalgam; so Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na, then Na + Hg → NaHg.
why: Step 1: normally H⁺ wins over Na⁺ (position in the series).
Step 2: the nature of the electrode changes this: discharge of H⁺ on Hg is very difficult.
Step 3: Na formed dissolves in Hg as amalgam NaHg(l), which removes it from the solution.
Step 4: Na⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Na(s); Na(s) + Hg(l) → NaHg(l).
questions.tip: This is the only common case where Na⁺ is discharged from water.

similar.a: An alloy of a metal with mercury.

questions.label: 2.2.4 Electrolysis of aqueous solutions

questions.q: CuSO₄(aq) is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. The solution at the end is …
why: Step 1: cathode removes Cu²⁺ (copper is deposited).
Step 2: anode removes OH⁻ (oxygen given off).
Step 3: H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ remain → sulphuric acid.
questions.tip: Look at which ions are left behind.

similar.q: Solution left after electrolysis of brine?

questions.label: 2.2.4 Electrolysis of aqueous solutions

questions.q: Write the half-equation at each electrode when CuSO₄(aq) is electrolysed with copper electrodes.
questions.answer: Cathode: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s); anode: Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻.
why: Step 1: cathode — Cu²⁺ is lower than H⁺ in the series → copper deposited.
Step 2: anode — the copper metal loses electrons more easily than SO₄²⁻ or OH⁻.
Step 3: so the anode dissolves; electrons balance (2 e⁻ each side).
questions.tip: An active anode dissolves instead of giving a gas.

similar.a: It increases by the same mass.

questions.label: 2.2.4 Electrolysis of aqueous solutions

questions.q: In concentrated hydrochloric acid, chloride ions are discharged at the anode in preference to hydroxide ions.
why: Step 1: OH⁻ is normally easier to discharge.
Step 2: in concentrated HCl, [Cl⁻] is enormously greater than [OH⁻].
Step 3: concentration wins → Cl₂.
questions.tip: High concentration can win over a small difference in the series.
questions.label: 2.2.4 Electrolysis of aqueous solutions

questions.q: Which electrolyte would you use to plate a spoon with silver?
why: Step 1: the electrolyte must contain the plating metal ions.
Step 2: silver → Ag⁺.
Step 3: silver nitrate is soluble → AgNO₃(aq).
questions.tip: Plating ion = plating metal.
questions.label: 2.2.5 Applications of electrolysis

questions.q: Write the electrode equations for the purification of copper and say what happens to the mass of each electrode.
questions.answer: Anode: Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ (loses mass). Cathode: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) (gains mass).
why: Step 1: impure copper anode dissolves.
Step 2: Cu²⁺ ions move to the pure cathode and are deposited.
Step 3: anode loses mass; cathode gains (slightly less, because impurities fall as mud).
questions.tip: Active anode → dissolves.
questions.label: 2.2.5 Applications of electrolysis

questions.q: The three products of the electrolysis of brine are …
why: Step 1: cathode H₂.
Step 2: anode Cl₂ (concentrated chloride).
Step 3: Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain → NaOH.
questions.tip: Brine → H₂ + Cl₂ + NaOH.
questions.label: 2.2.5 Applications of electrolysis

questions.q: Write the half-equations at the electrodes in the extraction of aluminium.
why: Step 1: molten electrolyte contains Al³⁺ and O²⁻.
Step 2: Al³⁺ gains 3 electrons at the cathode.
Step 3: O²⁻ loses 2 electrons; two of them give O₂.
Step 4: overall 2Al₂O₃(l) → 4Al(l) + 3O₂(g) (12 e⁻ transferred).
questions.tip: Balance electrons: 4Al³⁺ + 12e⁻ and 6O²⁻ − 12e⁻.

similar.q: Half-equation for sodium from molten NaCl?
Why must the electrolyte be molten?
similar.a: So that the ions can move.

questions.label: 2.2.5 Applications of electrolysis

questions.q: In electroplating with a silver anode the concentration of Ag⁺ in the electrolyte falls steadily.
why: Step 1: at the cathode Ag⁺ is removed.
Step 2: at the anode the same number of Ag⁺ ions is produced.
Step 3: the concentration stays constant.
questions.tip: Active anode replaces the ions used.
questions.label: 2.2.5 Applications of electrolysis

questions.q: What mass of silver is deposited by 0.50 A flowing for 30 minutes through AgNO₃(aq)? (Ag = 108)
why: Step 1: Ag⁺(aq) + e⁻ → Ag(s); z = 1.
questions.tip: Q = It with t in seconds.
questions.label: 2.2.6 Faraday's laws

questions.q: Exercise 2.9 Q1: find the mass of copper deposited from CuSO₄(aq) by a current of 2.0 A for 1 hour. (Cu = 63.5)
why: Step 1: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s); Eq. mass = 63.5/2 = 31.75 g.
questions.tip: Use the Eq. mass for a quick answer.

similar.q: Time to deposit 4.74 g with 2.0 A?

questions.label: 2.2.6 Faraday's laws

questions.q: Cells of AgNO₃ and CuSO₄ are in series. 1.08 g of silver is deposited. The mass of copper deposited (Cu = 64) is …
why: Step 1: Eq. masses: Ag 108/1 = 108; Cu 64/2 = 32.
questions.tip: Ratio of equivalent masses.

similar.q: Mass of Ni (Eq. 29.5) for the same charge?

questions.label: 2.2.6 Faraday's laws

questions.q: How long must 3.00 A flow to deposit 2.70 g of aluminium from molten Al₂O₃? (Al = 27)
questions.tip: moles of metal → moles of e⁻ → Q → t.
questions.label: 2.2.6 Faraday's laws

questions.q: In the electrolysis of dilute H₂SO₄, 0.0400 mol of electrons are passed. Find the moles of H₂ and of O₂ formed.
why: Step 1: cathode 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂: 2 e⁻ per H₂ → 0.0400/2 = 0.0200 mol.
Step 2: anode 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻: 4 e⁻ per O₂ → 0.0400/4 = 0.0100 mol.
Step 3: ratio 2 : 1.
questions.tip: Read the electrons off each half-equation.
questions.label: 2.2.6 Faraday's laws

questions.q: Doubling the current and halving the time leaves the mass deposited unchanged.
why: Step 1: m ∝ Q = I × t.
Step 3: Q is the same, so m is the same.
questions.tip: First law: mass depends only on the charge.
questions.label: 2.2.6 Faraday's laws
